title: Water sat around your Vero Beach house this week? A plain guide to gutters, downspouts and the swale out front
seoTitle: Vero Beach Drainage: Gutters, Downspouts and Swales
description: After this week's flooding, a simple Vero Beach guide to moving roof water away from your house: gutters, downspouts, the swale you maintain, and who to call.
dek: Monday's rain overwhelmed drainage in parts of Vero Beach. You cannot control the street, but you can control where your roof water goes. Here is what to look at once the water goes down, and who to call when it is not yours to fix.
facebook: Did water sit next to your Vero Beach house this week? The street drains are not the only thing that matters. Here's how to check your gutters, downspouts and the swale out front, plus who to call when the drainage problem isn't yours.

body.text: Monday's rain was too much for a lot of Vero Beach. CBS12 reported water covering roads, front lawns and driveways around 41st Avenue and 12th Street, with neighbors saying they had never seen flooding that bad there. The rain simply overwhelmed the drainage, and the water had nowhere to go but streets and yards.

Nobody can make a single house flood-proof in a storm like that. But this week is a good time to look at the part you do control: where the water from your own roof goes, and whether the grassy dip by the road is doing its job.

body.title: The short version
body.text: Keep gutters clear, point every downspout at lawn or plants that slope away from the house, never at the slab, driveway or street. Keep the swale in front of your home mowed and free of clippings and trash. Call the county or city when a road drain or ditch is the problem.

A roof collects a lot of rain and drops it in a few spots. If those spots are right next to the house, the water pools against the walls and the slab. Delaware's environmental agency, in its homeowner guide to extending downspouts, puts it simply: send the water downhill and away from the building, and do not let it pool next to it.

The University of Florida's Florida-Friendly Landscaping program gives the same advice with a Florida twist. Route gutters and downspouts into planted areas or other surfaces where water can soak in, so the rain stays on your lot instead of rushing off it.
Wait for a dry day and walk around the house. Look for these things:

items: Gutters full of leaves, palm debris or roof grit. Clogged gutters spill over the edge, right next to the wall.
Downspouts that leak at the seams or are blocked inside.
Downspouts that end at the foundation with no elbow or extension.
Downspouts that dump straight onto the driveway, sidewalk or street. The Delaware guide says not to let them flow directly onto paved surfaces.
Low spots where the yard tilts toward the house instead of away from it.
Stains, washed-out mulch or bare soil along the walls. Those show you where water has been sitting.

body.text: Most fixes are small. The Delaware guide estimated a downspout elbow at $7 to $25 and an extension at $7 to $30, in 2022 prices. Aim the extension at lawn or a planting bed that slopes away from the house. Gutter guards can cut down on leaf buildup if trees hang over your roof.

Thinking about a rain barrel? UF's Florida-Friendly program says that is fine if your HOA allows it, but use proper mosquito prevention. And if the yard needs regrading or new drainage, check with the city or county first about permits.
The swale out front is partly yours

Many Vero-area streets drain into swales: the shallow grassy dips between the road and your yard. Indian River County's stormwater FAQ explains that swales catch runoff from roads, slow it down and let it soak into the ground. Many are designed to hold water for up to 72 hours. So standing water in a swale for a day or two after a big rain is normal.

Here is the part many people do not know. The county says property owners handle the day-to-day care of swales in the easements around their property. That means mowing, keeping them clear, and not filling them in. A dry swale system that still has not drained after 72 hours may have a problem worth reporting.

Two easy habits help the whole street. Blow grass clippings back onto your lawn, not into the road, so they stay out of storm drains, as UF recommends. And keep trash and yard waste out of gutters and storm drains, as the county asks.
Who to call when it is not your problem

items: Inside Vero Beach city limits: start with the City of Vero Beach main line, (772) 978-5151.

Unincorporated Indian River County: to report flooding after rain, the county says to call its Road and Bridge Division at (772) 226-3460. Its service request page also covers road drainage, debris in the road and storm drain dumping.
Someone dumping into a swale, ditch or storm drain on county property: the county's Pollution Reporting System is (772) 226-1888, weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Not sure who is in charge? The county's main line is (772) 567-8000.
Take phone photos of where water stood around your house during the storm. They show you exactly where to look.
On a dry day, clear the gutters or have them cleared. Do not climb a ladder on wet ground or alone.
Check every downspout. Add an elbow and extension where water lands at the wall, and point it at lawn or plants that slope away.
Make sure no downspout empties onto the driveway, sidewalk or street.
Walk the swale out front. Pull out trash and clippings, and note whether it drains within about three days.
If a road drain, ditch or culvert is the problem, report it to the city or county using the numbers above.
Before any regrading or new drain work, ask the city or county whether a permit is needed.

faq.q: Who is responsible for the swale in front of my house in Indian River County?
faq.a: Indian River County says property owners handle the daily care and maintenance of swales in the easements around their property. The county's Road and Bridge Division maintains swales on county-owned property.

faq.q: How long should water stand in a swale after rain?
faq.a: The county says many swales are designed to hold water for up to 72 hours while it soaks in. A dry system that has not drained after 72 hours may not be working as designed.
Downhill and away from the house, into lawn or planted areas where water can soak in. Avoid sending them onto driveways, sidewalks or the street, and do not let water pool against the walls.

faq.q: Who do I call about flooding on my street in Vero Beach?
faq.a: Inside city limits, call the City of Vero Beach at (772) 978-5151. In unincorporated Indian River County, the county says to call Road and Bridge at (772) 226-3460 to report flooding after rain.

faq.q: Can I put a rain barrel on my downspout in Florida?
faq.a: UF's Florida-Friendly Landscaping program says you can use a rain barrel or cistern if your HOA permits it, with proper mosquito prevention.
